desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: In exhibit, teaching aid, or interactive product roles, look for contact with physical objects and actual users. Some roles hand off a drawing. Others follow the work through to an on-site trial.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If altering the sample yourself was the most interesting part, confirm that the job owns some of the hands-on work.
desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make something someone else can learn to use

ARS.career_lens: Follow a piece from concept to finished object. Who chooses the form and material, who builds it, and who watches how people use it? If you can participate in all three, find out whether you finish at delivery or revise it after people try it.
ARS.decision: If you want to try another form, look for design authority. If you'd rather improve how it is made or used, find chances to follow the sample into user testing.
ARS.headline: Turn an idea into a piece people can experience
ARS.hero_job_tip: In exhibition or experience design, find out who chooses the setting, builds the sample, and explains it to participants.
ARS.question: If a sample looks good and is hard to use, can a newcomer choose how to revise it and help build the next one?
ARS.scene: An exhibition can begin with a display board or with a model visitors can turn. You might want to choose what people encounter first. Those alternatives draw attention to different things. Once the model is built to scale, you can try it with visitors.
ARS.screen: Mark jobs where you decide the form of the final piece. Ask whether you can make a sample and observe someone using it.
ARS.trial: Sketch two paper sleeves that can be lifted with one hand. Build one, ask someone to pick it up, and mark what you would change.

ASR.career_lens: When an experience design role mentions creativity, ask whether you decide where participants start and how they interact. Find out whether you can lead a trial run and use the feedback to change displays, props, or visitor routes.
ASR.decision: If rearranging the experience interests you most, look for control over content. If you would rather guide people or make props, check typical time in those tasks.
ASR.headline: Find a new way to explain a confusing experience
ASR.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you can design the materials and coach participants, and who makes the tools they use.
ASR.question: When someone misses an interactive element, can a newcomer explain it again, adjust the prop, or change how the experience is arranged?
ASR.scene: You might be drawn to making an explanation work for the people taking part. Turn the instructions into a leaflet with one image per step, listen for confusion during practice, and update the leaflet and physical labels on the spot.
ASR.screen: Look for work where you design what participants do first and how to explain it. Ask if you will guide visitors and adjust props.
ASR.trial: Design a three-minute tabletop activity. Take someone through it and adjust one prop they didn't notice.

RAS.career_lens: In model, prop, or teaching aid jobs, first check whether you build a physical object from materials. Ask whether you can revise the design while building it and whether people get to try the sample. The answers show whether you would mainly build or also contribute to design and testing.
RAS.decision: If you want to build another sample, keep looking at production roles. If you want to change the shape or help people use it, check whether the job covers those parts.
RAS.headline: Build something people can use to practice
RAS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you would build on site, how much room you have to change the design, and whether you can see people using it.
RAS.question: After the first sample, would a newcomer try it with users and make changes based on what they see?
RAS.scene: A good teaching tool comes apart and goes together in your hands, while showing a beginner where every part fits. You might enjoy building one, marking the tricky pieces, and letting someone see whether they can use it independently.
RAS.screen: Look for making teaching tools or models by hand. Ask whether you can change the design during trial builds and let users try the finished piece.
RAS.trial: Make a movable sign out of cardstock, change its outline, and ask someone to use it to find a particular item. Record what wasn't obvious.

RSA.career_lens: Compare the time you spend setting up exhibits and helping at live activities. If visitor traffic stalls, do you guide people and change the signs yourself, or report the issue to another team?
RSA.decision: If you want to arrange the space again, prioritize on-site work. If you most want to greet people or design the signs, check how much time goes to each.
RSA.headline: Use the object in your hands to teach the movement
RSA.hero_job_tip: Check how much of the work involves handling objects and whether you can demonstrate and improve the teaching tools.
RSA.question: If visitors go the wrong way after an event starts, can a newcomer change the layout and signs? Who explains the change to visitors?
RSA.scene: You might enjoy a task you can try right away at the bench. Do it once yourself, let a newcomer practice, and use a color or sketch to mark the step that's easy to assemble backward.
RSA.screen: Mark jobs where you actually set things up, then check whether you guide people on site and update the signs.
RSA.trial: Set up two zones for a tabletop activity. Walk someone through both and add a sign to answer the question they actually had.

SAR.career_lens: Some support roles make diagrams or models to explain a task. Others answer questions on site using existing materials. Ask whether you meet users directly and whether you can make a sample for them to try.
SAR.decision: If you want to follow up on whether someone can now do it, explore direct support. If you prefer drawing or making, ask whether you can own that part.
SAR.headline: Turn a hard-to-explain instruction into a demonstration
SAR.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can meet learners and change the explanation, and how the job divides between making materials and showing the task in person.
SAR.question: When someone says the instructions make sense but still can't do it, can you make an example they can try?
SAR.scene: When someone can't follow “clip it to the side,” you might be willing to keep trying ways to explain until they can do it alone. Their response can tell you whether a sketch, a gesture, or a demonstration sample works best.
SAR.screen: Compare direct support with behind-the-scenes production. Look for jobs that let you understand a person's difficulty and revise the materials yourself.
SAR.trial: Ask someone which step is hardest to follow. Draw it and make a paper example they can handle.

SRA.career_lens: In practical training, learner independence can be one measure of success. Ask who demonstrates on the equipment, whether you practice with learners after mistakes, and whether you would revise the illustrations yourself.
SRA.decision: If you want to keep practicing with people, look at direct teaching. Check whether you can demonstrate with objects and update the materials too.
SRA.headline: Help someone go from understanding a task to doing it
SRA.hero_job_tip: In activity facilitation, ask how often you coach people directly, prepare materials, or adapt the tools yourself.
SRA.question: If the last learner couldn't operate independently, did the newcomer keep practicing with them, demonstrate again, or revise the illustration?
SRA.scene: Seeing someone make their first piece might make you want to keep teaching. Practice with materials beside them, resize a part that's awkward to hold, and color-code the sides that are easy to mix up.
SRA.screen: Look for jobs that coach people through an exercise and check whether they can do it alone. Ask whether demonstrations and producing materials belong to the same role.
SRA.trial: Guide someone through assembling a paper item and let them try independently. Draw a reminder for whichever part is easiest to reverse.

desktop_reading_v1.question: Once a sample is made, who watches how people use it and who can revise the next version?
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An interactive exhibit is built, but visitors don't know where to press. Change the physical buttons or the instructions and see whether a newcomer can use it on their own.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Check whether the job involves prototype building, experience design, and people using the item on site.
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make a paper mock-up of a button interface. Let someone try it and change a prompt where they got stuck.

top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.first_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a low-risk observation: in the first 10 minutes, bring materials, equipment, samples, or on-site constraints into view; in the next 10 minutes, try expression, naming, rewriting, layout, or a choice of form; in the final 10 minutes, clarify needs, points of confusion, or boundaries for collaboration with a real person. Record only which action you most want to continue.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.free_page_teaser: Realistic, Artistic, and Social interest clues can be observed in sequence without rushing to a career answer.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.likely_tension: Differences between the three clues are worth exploring through small tasks. Observing one action and one condition at a time is more reliable than treating the three leading interests as a fixed way of working.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.low_risk_validation: Low-risk observation: choose a small task that accommodates hands-on, expression, and support clues. Record the three activities separately and look only at activity preferences and evidence of wanting to continue.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.ordered_code_handling: The ordered three-letter code describes the reading order for this assessment: the first letter is the initial observation entry point, and the second and third are additional entry points. The order changes what to ask first and what to validate next. It is not a fixed identity, an ability conclusion, or a career answer.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Realistic focuses on tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results; Artistic focuses on expression, style, narrative, form, and experience; Social focuses on real people, understanding, support, communication, and collaboration. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.primary_activity_chain: Start with the first dimension, Realistic: use it as the initial observation entry point and look for small-task evidence involving tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.real_world_cost: Reading boundary: these three clues may occur in different parts of one task or across different environments. Record only the appeal of specific activities, points of hesitation, and conditions you want to adjust. Do not turn the score order into a ranking of abilities or a fixed way of working.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Artistic: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether expression, style, narrative, form, and experience make the task more appealing.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.strategy_label: Hands-on, expression, and support: three clues to observe
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Social, is only an additional clue: observe whether real people, understanding, support, communication, and collaboration help distinguish more specific task conditions.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.when_not_to_overread: When response quality is low, the leading scores are close, content is missing, or the user only wants to see the names, return to observing activities rather than offering strong interpretations.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.when_to_use_140q: When a user wants to distinguish whether task activities, environmental conditions, or role responsibilities are more appealing, 140Q can be an option. 140Q only adds contextual detail; it does not increase accuracy or override 60Q.

top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.activity_chain: Observe through three separate activity entry points: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions; try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form; observe goals, resources, opportunities, influence, or actions that move things forward.
activity_sequence: Initial observation entry point: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions
Second observation entry point: try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form
Third observation entry point: observe goals, resources, opportunities, influence, or actions that move things forward

They can help organize exploration and questions, but cannot establish a personality identity, ability level, or career conclusion.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.deep_report_extension: Further reading can distinguish preference evidence across tasks, environments, and role responsibilities, and offer exploration questions and follow-up actions.

desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Making a sample, preparing a presentation, and introducing a product are separate tasks. Ask what you actually get to make and whether convincing customers is a central measure of the job.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to iterate on samples and spend less of the week securing resources, prioritize roles with more production or design time.
desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make the sample and get a chance to try it

AER.career_lens: Some creative proposals go only as far as approval. Others require a budget, materials, and on-site setup. Ask whether you can change the physical result and whether the job is judged by the proposal, the event, or a commercial outcome.
AER.decision: If developing the idea appealed most, keep roles with time for creative work. If you want it funded and built, check how the team splits those duties.
AER.headline: Secure a chance to test a distinctive idea
AER.hero_job_tip: Ask what creative decisions you can make and how your time splits between pitching an idea and building it.
AER.question: Once a proposal is approved, does a newcomer stay involved through installation? What can they change when the budget is tight?
AER.scene: You might enjoy coming up with a stand that stands out. Once the idea is clear, ask the organizers for space and budget. Use a small model to show what the structure and installation will require.
AER.screen: Mark which presentation decisions you would lead. Find out whether you also seek budget approval or set up the work on site.
AER.trial: Design a small exhibit and sketch what people see first. Agree on budget limits, then mock it up using what you have.

ARE.career_lens: In product styling or installation design, ask which aspects of the appearance and experience you decide. Find out whether you make a sample yourself, explain the trade-offs in a review, and request time for another build.
ARE.decision: If you want to keep designing and building, look for creative decision-making. If the presentation and approval interested you more, check how success is assessed.
ARE.headline: Show what you want to make with a sample
ARE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you would take a design from concept to sample and whether you contribute to the proposal or own getting it approved.
ARE.question: At the last creative review, could a newcomer bring their own sample and explain the trade-offs? Who took over the revisions after feedback?
ARE.scene: You might be most interested in giving the product its form and feel. Putting a sample on site reveals what fits. Then you can show the person responsible how the versions differ and discuss which to keep.
ARE.screen: Look for roles that can choose the form, make a sample, and present it for approval.
ARE.trial: Sketch two shapes for a display object, make one out of paper, and use it to explain your decision and ask for a trial installation.

EAR.career_lens: For creative roles with a business development focus, ask what counts as getting a project off the ground: signing a partner, delivering a proposal, or producing a usable sample. Different people often own each milestone.
EAR.decision: If you liked getting a partner on board, look for roles responsible for adoption. If preparing the proposal or building the sample appealed more, look for clear ownership of that output.
EAR.headline: Get support for a proposal so it can actually happen
EAR.hero_job_tip: Compare how much time goes into securing resources, creating a proposal, and taking part in a trial build.
EAR.question: After an agreement, can the person who started it decide what to show and check a sample, or do the design and production teams take over?
EAR.scene: Finding someone to provide space, funding, and time may be the part you most want to own. Show different ways to explain what the project would do, then use a sample to make the trade-offs in size, materials, or assembly visible.
EAR.screen: Determine whether the job mainly wins partners, sets the proposal's direction, or makes a sample people can see. Ask who owns each part.
EAR.trial: Write two partnership terms for an imaginary market. Make a one-page proposal and test part of a stall layout with paper.

ERA.career_lens: An event lead might set deadlines, coordinate suppliers, and oversee installation, or mainly get approval. Ask whether you handle constraints in person and who decides changes to visitor routes or displays.
ERA.decision: If you wanted to get everyone working to the new plan, explore delivery coordination. If building or the look of the outcome mattered most, check dedicated roles in those areas.
ERA.headline: Turn an agreement into something visible on site
ERA.hero_job_tip: Find out whether results mean closing a deal or delivering the project, and whether you can work on the physical solution.
ERA.question: The last time a display changed at short notice, who reassigned tasks and who could change the size or display order on site?
ERA.scene: You might enjoy turning a customer's vague request into something both sides can agree to deliver. Use a working prototype to set the scope and ask a designer to show two versions of a detail so the customer can see what they are choosing.
ERA.screen: Find project roles that schedule the venue, staff, and work. Ask whether they also help install the display and revise its design.
ERA.trial: Simulate a smaller venue. Reassign tasks between two people, shrink the layout, and draw a route visitors can still follow.

RAE.career_lens: Compare the time spent building a sample, changing its shape, and explaining it to others. Ask whether your responsibility ends with the sample or continues until a customer agrees to use it.
RAE.decision: If you want to keep making samples, prioritize prototype production. If seeing it adopted matters most, ask whether demonstrations and partner discussions are secondary tasks or measures of success.
RAE.headline: Build a prototype that captures the idea
RAE.hero_job_tip: For sample development roles, ask how much you build yourself and how much time you spend pitching a design or securing a budget.
RAE.question: After a newcomer makes a sample, do they change how it is presented, demonstrate it, and find out whether it is adopted?
RAE.scene: Between a sketch and a working sample, you may most enjoy trying out materials, dimensions, and assembly methods. Once the sample works, refine its form and material and bring it, along with the cost trade-offs, to ask for another round of prototypes.
RAE.screen: Use the stated deliverables to tell whether the work mainly builds samples, revises appearance, or presents the product and wins orders.
RAE.trial: Make a paper sample and change its appearance. Prepare a 30-second demonstration and ask someone if they would try it and why.

REA.career_lens: Some changes can be made by the person building the item. Others need permission from a venue or organizer. Ask who made the last decision and whether you can still change how the finished item is presented.
REA.decision: To keep solving physical space problems, look for installation duties. If negotiating the conditions was more appealing, also compare field coordination.
REA.headline: Use a physical sample to deliver on an improvement proposal
REA.hero_job_tip: Look for roles where you can deliver an improvement and help it get adopted. Ask whether you decide how to present it.
REA.question: If the space gets smaller at short notice, can a newcomer try another setup, negotiate a time to make changes, and rearrange it?
REA.scene: You might want to change a device that feels awkward to use. Show the revised part to the person responsible, explain the time and materials it needs, and use a label or detail in the shape to make the new use clear.
REA.screen: Find jobs that build on site and handle changes. Check whether you negotiate with the venue and revise the displays yourself.
REA.trial: Use two sheets of paper to represent two sites. Set up a display and ask someone playing the venue owner to give you a restriction. Make a second version that works within it.

desktop_reading_v1.question: On the last proposal, did the person who made the sample also present it and help decide what to keep?
desktop_reading_v1.scene: A product could have two shapes. Make two rough versions people can hold, decide how to show the difference, and ask the team to try selling one of them.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare sample building, visual presentation, and delivering proposals. Some roles own only one.
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make two paper prototypes for the same small object. Outline how each would be used and one reason to test it.

desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Prototyping a product and maintaining its specifications can both require knowing the material. Ask whether you can change its construction and appearance or mostly check whether finished items meet the existing specifications.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to make new samples, look closely at the prototype work. If you also want to keep production consistent, compare process and quality roles.
desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make a prototype possible to reproduce

ACR.career_lens: A visual project may involve deciding proportions, colors, and layouts or mainly managing versions and material specifications. Ask whether checking a physical sample on site is also part of the job.
ACR.decision: If choosing how to present things mattered most, look for creative discretion. If you also want to maintain standards and inspect physical samples, check for both responsibilities.
ACR.headline: Turn a visual approach into standards the next person can use
ACR.hero_job_tip: Check whether the job lets you set design principles, maintain the standards, and help build the physical sample.
ACR.question: When a template is used on a new material, can the designer adjust the rule and verify a sample?
ACR.scene: You might enjoy setting the layout and colors for a packaging range. Give the different sizes a shared labeling system, then check the first physical production run to see which design details still need work.
ACR.screen: Compare design choices with maintaining standards. Ask whether you can take a sample to the actual site and check it there.
ACR.trial: Make two signs for the same topic, with rules for type size and numbering. View them at different distances and note which specification should change.

ARC.career_lens: A job that turns concepts into reproducible small runs can involve trial builds, refining the appearance, and writing specifications. Ask whether you decide how it looks and stay involved in testing production after the design is approved.
ARC.decision: If you want to try another form, look for design ownership. If adjustment or consistency interested you more, compare time in production and keeping specifications current.
ARC.headline: Make a design ready to build and deliver
ARC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can refine the design alongside the prototype and whether you set or follow the delivery requirements.
ARC.question: After the design is approved, does a newcomer check a second build and revise the dimensional notes?
ARC.scene: You might care most about the form, proportions, and feel of different materials. Build a sample to inspect the seams, then put the details that matter into the specifications so the piece retains its character after handover.
ARC.screen: Look for creative roles that design the form, make the first item, and provide reproducible specifications. Distinguish concept work from production handover.
ARC.trial: Sketch two shapes for a paper nameplate and make one of them. Write three specifications and ask someone to reproduce it from the instructions.

CAR.career_lens: In records or standards management, you might make a diagram others can act on. Ask whether you only issue new versions or also check signs and samples on site and revise the instructions when something doesn't match.
CAR.decision: If maintaining clear rules appealed most, start with records or standards. If you preferred drawing instructions or inspecting items, compare how much time those take.
CAR.headline: Build an operating standard people will actually use
CAR.hero_job_tip: In process roles, find out who manages documents, designs instructions, and checks the work in person.
CAR.question: When an instruction and the physical item show different versions for the same reference number, can this role inspect the item and revise the guidance?
CAR.scene: You might catch the same rule written differently in three documents. Bring the reference numbers and versions into line, make a visual guide for the key steps, and walk through it beside the equipment to see what needs changing.
CAR.screen: Look for version control, classification, and maintaining standards. Check whether you also make visual instructions and can verify them in person.
CAR.trial: Organize five objects by category and sketch where to find them. Verify the drawing, reference numbers, and physical locations one by one.

CRA.career_lens: Acceptance checks bring together the physical item, work order, and specifications. If you also want to make the documentation easier to use, find out whether you could redraw labels or checklists and personally inspect parts that failed.
CRA.decision: If you want to keep inspecting and documenting items, start with quality or inventory roles. If changing a label was more appealing, check for information design duties.
CRA.headline: Straighten out a process that keeps going wrong
CRA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you inspect to a standard or also take part on site and change how instructions are presented.
CRA.question: If handover records and item labels disagree, can a newcomer check the site and remake the labels?
CRA.scene: You might want each step to have a standard others can check. Verify where tools sit and how each step is performed at the workbench. Then choose a clearer diagram for the handover.
CRA.screen: Look for jobs that check lists and sign off deliveries. Find out whether you inspect the physical items and improve labels people confuse.
CRA.trial: Make an inventory checklist for a box of stationery, inspect each item, and redraw the label that would be easiest to put in the wrong place.

RAC.career_lens: Some production jobs let you adjust appearance while building. Others follow a finished design. Ask what you can change on one actual sample, what you have to document, and whether someone else can reproduce it.
RAC.decision: If you want to keep testing materials and making things, prioritize production. If appearance or repeatability mattered more, check who owns the design or maintains the specifications.
RAC.headline: Make something attractive that others can reproduce
RAC.hero_job_tip: Ask how much time goes to prototyping and who sets the form and the production specifications.
RAC.question: When a sample's outline changed at the last minute, did a newcomer rebuild it from the drawing or also update the drawing and version record?
RAC.scene: You might want to build a sample that works. After choosing its shape and finish, document the dimensions and assembly steps that affect the appearance so the next one can match.
RAC.screen: Check weekly production time, how much you can change the presentation, and whether you document specifications so someone can build it again.
RAC.trial: Make two paper holders. Change the outline of the first and write a dimensions-and-steps card to see if it can be reproduced in the second.

RCA.career_lens: Some fabrication and assembly jobs mainly deliver consistent, traceable work. If you also want to contribute to design, ask whether you can propose a new fixture when one doesn't work well or only record the exception.
RCA.decision: If you want to repeat the work and check it against specifications, look at production roles. If you mainly want to change the structure, check who owns those design decisions.
RCA.headline: Refine a repeated task at the workbench
RCA.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you mainly operate equipment or maintain standards, and whether you can improve the workstation or its instructions.
RCA.question: If an item meets its specifications and is still hard to use, can a newcomer propose changing the structure or only document the issue and pass it on?
RCA.scene: You might enjoy working with tools and materials directly. Rearrange parts people keep picking up by mistake, record the right order, and change the labels so others can find what they need at a glance.
RCA.screen: Mark duties that work to specifications and record deviations. Ask whether you can propose smaller design changes within those rules.
RCA.trial: Make three paper parts to one size and list the checks for acceptance. If one is hard to handle, sketch a change that preserves the important dimensions.

desktop_reading_v1.question: After a design changes, who turns the revised sample into specifications and acceptance checks others can use?
desktop_reading_v1.scene: A display stand looks good but is hard to reassemble at each site. Revise the joint and the appearance, then document measurements and acceptance checks.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Find out whether the prototype role owns its appearance, construction, and handover specifications or mainly builds to a drawing.
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make a folding model from paper. Draw the assembly steps and try building it again from your instructions alone.

desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Event operations, service coordination, and equipment operation can appear in one posting. Find out whether the role mainly solves on-site problems, coaches new people, or schedules resources to get the work done.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you want to guide a team without spending most days responding to emergencies, ask how often unplanned work comes up and how teams hand it over.
desktop_reading_v1.headline: Help people get something working on site

ERS.career_lens: For on-site project work, distinguish organizing staff, building the setup, and solving problems participants encounter. When the venue changed at short notice, did this role reschedule and assign work or also get equipment in place and restore the service?
ERS.decision: If you want to follow the changes through on site, look for coordination authority and access to outcomes. If hands-on setup or helping participants mattered most, seek out that primary responsibility.
ERS.headline: Negotiate a workable plan for an on-site improvement
ERS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the role ends at agreeing on plans and results or also involves carrying them out and coaching people afterward.
ERS.question: After the last venue change, did a newcomer reschedule staff, help set up, or mainly notify people?
ERS.scene: You might prefer getting several groups to make an improvement possible. Walk the person responsible through the equipment change, then arrange a handover that leaves the people using it time to learn.
ERS.screen: Find jobs that explicitly assign on-site duties and resources. Check whether the coordinator physically helps set up or works directly with participants.
ERS.trial: Pretend the venue has shrunk by half. Reassign two duties, set up a small help point, and ask someone to try the route.

ESR.career_lens: Find out whether people leading projects on the front line can use feedback to arrange resources. Some mainly recruit and coordinate; others check the equipment and space in person and make changes happen.
ESR.decision: If securing help and making the plan work appealed most, keep jobs with real coordination responsibility. If participant requests or physical changes drew you in, check the time given to those tasks.
ESR.headline: Get people to adopt a new on-site procedure
ESR.hero_job_tip: Check whether your main responsibility is getting people to adopt a practice, and whether you would work directly with users and equipment.
ESR.question: After staffing is sorted, does a newcomer have time to hear what participants need and change the setup?
ESR.scene: You might be drawn to getting several shifts to agree to try a new procedure. Find out what support operators need, demonstrate the equipment, and use their feedback to plan what happens next with a supervisor.
ESR.screen: Compare recruitment and staffing duties, then ask whether you can hear directly from participants and help make on-site changes.
ESR.trial: Ask someone to pose two participant needs. Negotiate one workable arrangement and draw the visitor route to see if it accommodates them.

RES.career_lens: When a service moves to a new site, you might install and test equipment, arrange handover, and set aside time for users to practice. Find out if you deliver working equipment or stay until people are ready to take it over.
RES.decision: If you want to set things up and hand them over, look at implementation roles. If you preferred arranging the trial or teaching others, check the time those duties get.
RES.headline: Get an on-site change through handover
RES.hero_job_tip: Find out how far you would take a repair yourself and whether you would also coordinate downtime or training.
RES.question: After equipment is working, must a newcomer arrange the handover and run through operation with users before the job is complete?
RES.scene: You might prefer fixing a fault you can handle yourself. After the repair, agree when teams can switch equipment. Ask the next shift to operate it while you watch for any step that still needs a reminder.
RES.screen: See what an implementation job installs or adjusts directly. Ask whether handover and helping people get started are part of acceptance.
RES.trial: Rearrange a shared item, make time to try it, and show someone how to use it. Write down what you missed in the handover.

RSE.career_lens: Some on-site service shifts focus on equipment checks. Others also help visitors through practical difficulties while operating it. Ask whether you refer problems beyond your authority or contact the people who can resolve them.
RSE.decision: If you want to solve hands-on problems, keep roles centered on operations. If serving people or coordinating appealed more, find out how regularly those tasks come up.
RSE.headline: Finish the job and show teammates how to do it
RSE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can both operate equipment and teach others to use it. Find out how much coordination you would own.
RSE.question: When a tool becomes unavailable, does a newcomer handle the equipment and help visitors? Who handles issues beyond their authority?
RSE.scene: You might first want to fit the troublesome part on site. Let the person taking over try it once. If they need a shared tool that isn't available, talk to the person responsible about access and timing.
RSE.screen: Mark operating equipment and troubleshooting in person. See whether you also help visitors directly or arrange other staff.
RSE.trial: Set up a tabletop service desk. Ask someone to simulate having trouble collecting an item, clear the obstacle, and agree on a backup plan.

SER.career_lens: In service project coordination, find out whether you hear directly what participants need. Then ask if you decide how to allocate support or rearrange seating, equipment, or access on site. These responsibilities can belong to separate teams.
SER.decision: If you want ongoing contact with participants, keep jobs combining service and coordination. If you most enjoy getting the setup right, look at event operations.
SER.headline: Arrange the support a group needs
SER.hero_job_tip: Compare time spent supporting employees directly and securing commitments across departments. Ask if you can demonstrate on site.
SER.question: When a participant explains a difficulty, can this role arrange help or make changes on site, or can it only respond to them?
SER.scene: You might notice that new colleagues keep asking for help with one step they haven't practiced. Pull together what they say, get some training time approved, and work through the step with them and the actual tools.
SER.screen: Look for direct service and arranging resources. Find out whether you also prepare the venue or equipment.
SER.trial: Plan a tabletop activity for someone. Ask what they need, agree how you can help, and try setting the activity up.

SRE.career_lens: For community facilities or activity support, ask for one example of a request for help. Did the person in the role explain how to use something, go on site and adjust it, or coordinate with others to remove an obstacle? Where the task ends tells you what the work involves.
SRE.decision: If you want to follow up with the person, keep direct support jobs. If you preferred fixing the setup or coordinating the response, check who owns those tasks.
SRE.headline: Help a team start using a new tool
SRE.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you would teach on site and whether you'd need to get training time or equipment approved.
SRE.question: If someone can't use the event equipment easily, can a newcomer try a different layout with them? Who can help with resources?
SRE.scene: You might care most about whether everyone can use a tool independently. Listen to what confuses them, practice with them, then talk to a supervisor about setting time aside for practice.
SRE.screen: Find work that helps participants in person. See whether an obstacle calls for changing the setup or getting other people involved.
SRE.trial: Have someone try to pick up items from a shared desk. Listen, remove one obstacle, and agree on who will maintain the new setup.

desktop_reading_v1.question: When something goes wrong before an event, does someone in this role diagnose the equipment problem and help beginners, or mostly coordinate the response?
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An event is about to start. Equipment isn't ready and volunteers aren't sure what to do. The work can involve adjusting the equipment, showing people how to use it, and changing who handles what.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Find out whether the role focuses on working on site, training people, or being accountable for the schedule and coordination.
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a familiar everyday tool. Make a quick-start card and assign on-site responsibilities for a small group task.

top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.first_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a low-risk observation: in the first 10 minutes, bring materials, equipment, samples, or on-site constraints into view; in the next 10 minutes, clarify needs, points of confusion, or boundaries for collaboration with a real person; in the final 10 minutes, clarify the goal, resources, next step, and people you need to influence. Record only which action you most want to continue.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.free_page_teaser: Realistic, Social, and Enterprising interest clues can be observed in sequence without rushing to a career answer.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.likely_tension: Differences between the three clues are worth exploring through small tasks. Observing one action and one condition at a time is more reliable than treating the three leading interests as a fixed way of working.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.low_risk_validation: Low-risk observation: choose a small task that accommodates hands-on, support, and moving things forward clues. Record the three activities separately and look only at activity preferences and evidence of wanting to continue.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.ordered_code_handling: The ordered three-letter code describes the reading order for this assessment: the first letter is the initial observation entry point, and the second and third are additional entry points. The order changes what to ask first and what to validate next. It is not a fixed identity, an ability conclusion, or a career answer.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Realistic focuses on tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results; Social focuses on real people, understanding, support, communication, and collaboration; Enterprising focuses on goals, resources, opportunities, influence, and moving things forward. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.primary_activity_chain: Start with the first dimension, Realistic: use it as the initial observation entry point and look for small-task evidence involving tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.real_world_cost: Reading boundary: these three clues may occur in different parts of one task or across different environments. Record only the appeal of specific activities, points of hesitation, and conditions you want to adjust. Do not turn the score order into a ranking of abilities or a fixed way of working.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Social: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether real people, understanding, support, communication, and collaboration make the task more appealing.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.strategy_label: Hands-on, support, and moving things forward: three clues to observe
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Enterprising, is only an additional clue: observe whether goals, resources, opportunities, influence, and moving things forward help distinguish more specific task conditions.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.when_not_to_overread: When response quality is low, the leading scores are close, content is missing, or the user only wants to see the names, return to observing activities rather than offering strong interpretations.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.when_to_use_140q: When a user wants to distinguish whether task activities, environmental conditions, or role responsibilities are more appealing, 140Q can be an option. 140Q only adds contextual detail; it does not increase accuracy or override 60Q.

top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.activity_chain: Observe through three separate activity entry points: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions; observe real people's needs for understanding, support, communication, or collaboration; organize rules, data, processes, order, or reviewable records.
activity_sequence: Initial observation entry point: work with tangible objects, tools, or on-site conditions
Second observation entry point: observe real people's needs for understanding, support, communication, or collaboration
Third observation entry point: organize rules, data, processes, order, or reviewable records
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.core_reading: These three leading interest dimensions indicate that Realistic, Social, and Conventional activities stand relatively high in this response. They can help organize exploration and questions, but cannot establish a personality identity, ability level, or career conclusion.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.deep_report_extension: Further reading can distinguish preference evidence across tasks, environments, and role responsibilities, and offer exploration questions and follow-up actions.

desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: On-site coaching can center on demonstrating a procedure or on reviewing records. Compare postings that explicitly mention coaching beginners in person, making checklists, or updating operating instructions.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If demonstrating and correcting a mistake appealed most, look first at coaching duties. If you wanted to establish a consistent standard, look at process responsibilities.
desktop_reading_v1.headline: Make on-site work easy to hand over

CRS.career_lens: For store handover or equipment management, a good result means the physical items, system records, and next person's understanding match. Find out whether you spend most days checking items or also turn gaps you find into steps for training the next shift.
CRS.decision: If matching records to physical items was appealing, keep inventory or quality handover jobs. If you want to teach on site, ask about coaching new colleagues.
CRS.headline: Give operations and handovers standards people can follow
CRS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you help set the standard and how much time goes to on-site verification and coaching newcomers.
CRS.question: When an inventory check finds conflicting records, does this role verify on site and show the next shift what to check?
CRS.scene: You might pay attention to whether people on the next shift can see what the current shift did. Walk through the task, choose the checks that must be recorded, and teach a newcomer how to fill in and verify the record.
CRS.screen: Look for inspections and records. Check whether you verify the items in person and coach the next shift or mainly check the system.
CRS.trial: Count five items using a checklist. Pick an unclear instruction, check it together, and revise the record.

CSR.career_lens: For a service process role, ask who sets intake rules and who helps people who get stuck trying to follow them. When registration causes problems, find out whether you adjust the equipment on site or hand it to operations.
CSR.decision: If keeping the rules clear appeals, look at process work. If helping people in person was more interesting, find out how the role reaches actual users.
CSR.headline: Organize a service so support continues when another person takes over
CSR.hero_job_tip: Check whether you mainly deliver reliable records or practice with people directly and how much of either involves working on site.
CSR.question: When people repeatedly ask for help at the same step, can you change the checklist and try the new procedure with users on site?
CSR.scene: If the handover omits what a learner has tried, the next colleague has to ask them from the beginning. You could clarify the record so somebody else can keep helping. If the problem needs showing, bring the actual equipment.
CSR.screen: Find roles that manage verification procedures. Ask whether they also work with users and can change how equipment is arranged.
CSR.trial: Write borrowing and return rules for shared stationery. Ask someone to try them, handle one exception, and change part of the layout.

RCS.career_lens: Operating roles need records. Ask how much of a shift goes to keeping them and whether they're an aid or the main output. If you want to pass on field experience, check for time to train colleagues or revise instructions.
RCS.decision: If both building and checking appealed, keep field roles with clear handover duties. If you wanted to explain it to others, check how much training you get to do.
RCS.headline: Finish the hands-on work and leave the key steps for the next shift
RCS.hero_job_tip: Find out how an ordinary day splits between hands-on tasks, checklist checks, and training whoever takes over.
RCS.question: If the record passed but the equipment looks wrong, does a newcomer check it personally and explain it to the next shift?
RCS.scene: Once you have checked an item, can the next person tell immediately what needs to happen? The handover may be part of what interests you. Mark what needs rework against a shared standard, then check it together on site so the next shift can see what the checklist means.
RCS.screen: Compare time operating equipment and keeping itemized records. Check whether you teach people to follow the process.
RCS.trial: Assemble a paper model, check three items on a list, and show someone how to use the list to check the finished model.

RSC.career_lens: For equipment or facility operations, ask whether you check and fix things yourself. If you also train newcomers, find out whether you demonstrate occasionally or are responsible for independent operation and updating the handover checklist.
RSC.decision: If you want to keep doing the task directly, look for field operations. If you want to teach or improve the checklist, look for real time in those tasks.
RSC.headline: Teach on-site operations well enough for a confident handover
RSC.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the job combines operating equipment with training others, and which records you update each shift.
RSC.question: From shadowing to independent work, who demonstrates, verifies a newcomer's work, and updates the records?
RSC.scene: You might like work where you have tools in your hands and can see the result. Demonstrate an inspection to a newcomer, explain safety limits while they practice, and note easily missed checks on the handover sheet.
RSC.screen: Find jobs with hands-on inspections or operation, and mark whether you also demonstrate procedures and fill out handover checks.
RSC.trial: Organize some stationery, inspect it, and show someone how to repeat the process. Write a three-line checklist of what they missed.

SCR.career_lens: Service follow-up often involves recording who handles a case next. Ask whether you can show people how to use the real object as well as answering questions and updating records, or mostly work by phone with existing instructions.
SCR.decision: If you want to keep answering and following up, explore support. If clear handovers or field operations appealed more, compare time spent on each.
SCR.headline: Make sure anyone who asks for help gets follow-up
SCR.hero_job_tip: In a support job, compare how much time goes into follow-up, record keeping, and demonstrating a task on site.
SCR.question: When a request needs follow-up across shifts, can a newcomer demonstrate a solution? What information goes into the handover?
SCR.scene: Support is hard to continue if someone has to tell the same story every time they ask for help. You might want to track where they struggle and how far they have practiced. At the next session, you can open the record and start at the step they couldn't get past.
SCR.screen: Find jobs that answer questions and maintain follow-up records. Ask whether you sometimes demonstrate with the real equipment.
SCR.trial: Ask someone for a question about a familiar tool. Demonstrate the answer and leave a note a colleague could use to continue helping.

SRC.career_lens: Ask what a training role delivers after a session. If it includes demonstrating, coaching, recording progress, and handing over steps people still need help with, your work continues beyond the initial explanation.
SRC.decision: If you want to coach another round, prioritize practical training. If making the object or recording progress mattered more, find roles where that is central.
SRC.headline: Coach someone until they can operate independently
SRC.hero_job_tip: Ask who sets up repeated practice, provides actual equipment, and tracks progress in a coaching role.
SRC.question: How does a coach know a learner can work independently? Do newcomers get to demonstrate and record progress?
SRC.scene: You might care most about the moment someone no longer needs help. Let them practice with real tools and put the easy-to-miss checks on one list for them to use afterward.
SRC.screen: Find jobs that coach people directly. Check whether you demonstrate in person and record progress.
SRC.trial: Teach someone a familiar craft and let them do it alone. Record where they needed a prompt and where they didn't.

desktop_reading_v1.question: When can someone new usually operate on their own? How often do you update checklists in response to what happens on site?
desktop_reading_v1.scene: New colleagues understand the procedure and still skip the final check. Show them how to do it, leave a checklist, and observe what people still miss after training.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Look at operating equipment, coaching people, and keeping records. Identify which activity you want to do regularly.
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Make a five-step handover card for a familiar, safe task. Ask a colleague to explain the steps using the card.

desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Project delivery and quality management can both include final acceptance. Project delivery often involves resolving delays and assigning responsibilities. Quality management checks that the physical work and the records agree.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If coordinating was most appealing, check whether the role can set priorities. If you wanted to make the handover reliable, check whether you can change the process.
desktop_reading_v1.headline: Follow the plan through to on-site delivery

CER.career_lens: Writing intake and acceptance rules takes time, and so does getting everyone to follow them. If you want both duties, ask who negotiates revised dates with suppliers and when you would verify results on site.
CER.decision: If you want to set clear rules and follow up on them, keep roles that combine standards maintenance with coordination. If you also want hands-on work, ask how much is done on site.
CER.headline: Check who owes what and what actually got delivered
CER.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you mainly track records or can also request corrective work and verify the result on site.
CER.question: When a delivery misses the acceptance criteria, can a newcomer reset deadlines and responsibilities, or do they only record the exception? Would they recheck the item in person?
CER.scene: You might want to reconcile what the contract, work order, and acceptance record each say. After seeing the condition of the equipment, you can confirm what is incomplete and which party can arrange the fix.
CER.screen: Look for jobs that maintain standards and coordinate their use. Check whether you would personally re-inspect what is being signed off.
CER.trial: Write three standards for a desk setup, agree on when changes are due, and then check the setup against each standard and record the exceptions.

CRE.career_lens: A quality role can decide whether work meets a standard or follow up to get it corrected. Ask whether you inspect physical items and coordinate a fix when the same issue comes up repeatedly.
CRE.decision: If you want to make records easy to verify, consider process quality. If you want to change equipment or coordinate corrective work, check access to the site and authority to propose changes.
CRE.headline: Use inspection records to drive equipment improvements
CRE.hero_job_tip: In inspection or quality roles, ask whether you help design the checks and how far you can follow up on what you find.
CRE.question: Who noticed a required item missing from the maintenance form? Could a newcomer inspect the equipment and get the form changed?
CRE.scene: How many repairs were made, and which one worked? You might want to make each inspection traceable. Once you check the equipment on site against the same standard, the records give you something concrete to discuss with the person deciding which repairs come first.
CRE.screen: Look for roles that maintain checklists, inspect equipment, and request corrections. Distinguish completing the form from being able to change it.
CRE.trial: Make an equipment repair form and run two items through it. Find a gap and propose a change to the form.

ECR.career_lens: For delivery management jobs, find out whether performance is judged on securing commitments up front or documenting delivery and acceptance at the end. If you want contact with the equipment itself, ask whether you can go on site to check a disputed delivery.
ECR.decision: If following through on commitments was the part you wanted to own, keep jobs with coordination and sign-off responsibilities. If you mainly wanted to document or inspect the delivery, look for roles that make room for those duties.
ECR.headline: Turn an agreed goal into a delivery everyone can verify
ECR.hero_job_tip: Ask whether the job centers on reaching agreement or also includes setting acceptance rules and joining on-site checks.
ECR.question: The last time a supplier was late, could a newcomer renegotiate the deadline, update acceptance conditions, and verify the delivery on site?
ECR.scene: You may be drawn to getting several parties behind the same goal. Once you agree on who's responsible and when it is due, put the commitments on an acceptance checklist and see whether the installed equipment meets it in person.
ECR.screen: Check who sets the order of work and who signs off. Look separately at commitments, acceptance rules, and on-site verification.
ECR.trial: Imagine two shipments will arrive late. Agree on priorities with someone, write one page of responsibilities and acceptance checks, and run through it with objects on a desk.

ERC.career_lens: For project delivery, ask who negotiates dates and who resolves on-site problems. If you want to work with equipment or materials, use a recent handover to see whether you would inspect the physical work or collect signatures and follow up on progress.
ERC.decision: If you want to own the commitment and see the result on site, keep coordination roles with acceptance duties. If you prefer installation or checking, look for that core responsibility.
ERC.headline: Turn requests from several sites into one upgrade the team can deliver
ERC.hero_job_tip: In project roles, ask whether you negotiate downtime, budgets, and responsibilities and whether you follow test fits on site.
ERC.question: When delivery dates conflict, can the lead reassign responsibility? Does acceptance mean inspecting the work or collecting signatures?
ERC.scene: Several shifts want the equipment upgraded and none wants to give up production time. You might be most drawn to getting those groups to agree. Use a sample modification to show the plan and agree on the acceptance and handover rules.
ERC.screen: Mark jobs that coordinate staff to meet a deadline. Ask whether they also set up and inspect work on site.
ERC.trial: Simulate a tabletop installation. Agree on who does what and by when, handle one part, and check it against agreed conditions.

RCE.career_lens: For fixture, facility, or equipment improvement jobs, ask what you modify yourself. Some also update operating records and ask the team to try a new approach. If the focus is promoting adoption, the hands-on component can be smaller than the title suggests.
RCE.decision: If you want hands-on work and fewer repeated mistakes, keep field jobs with handover ownership. If getting others to adopt changes appealed more, look for roles that own that work.
RCE.headline: Make every repair traceable
RCE.hero_job_tip: Find out who owns routine maintenance, handles exceptions, and requests upgrades.
RCE.question: The last time a shop-floor change became a procedure, who made it, documented it, and persuaded the next shift to try it?
RCE.scene: You might want to restore a machine against clear standards. If the same part keeps failing, record readings before and after each repair, then use those findings to discuss a replacement or upgrade.
RCE.screen: Look for jobs with hands-on checks and adjustments and responsibility for handover rules. Ask whether you also help others adopt the changes.
RCE.trial: Rearrange a set of tools and write three rules for putting them back. Ask someone to try them and point out one rule that doesn't work.

REC.career_lens: When an implementation job owns delivery, ask whether you personally install or configure equipment, and whether you can reschedule if there is a conflict. Check whether you document tests, omissions, and sign-off or hand over once installation is done.
REC.decision: If building was most engaging, look for jobs with hands-on time. If scheduling or checking delivery appealed more, ask what authority the role has.
REC.headline: Carry an equipment upgrade through to on-site delivery
REC.hero_job_tip: Start with roles that own physical changes. Ask how much time then goes to coordinating downtime and documenting acceptance.
REC.question: When the last installation ran out of time, could a newcomer rearrange tasks and document acceptance criteria?
REC.scene: You might want to fix a device that keeps failing. The machine needs downtime, so agree on a window with production and document the replacement parts and acceptance checks.
REC.screen: Check whether you carry out installations yourself. Find out whether rescheduling people and accepting the delivery are core duties or things you help with.
REC.trial: Use paper parts to simulate assembly. If something is missing, change the order and write a handover record the next shift can verify.

desktop_reading_v1.question: When delivery ran late last time, could this role revise the schedule or inspection method, or did it mainly update the status?
desktop_reading_v1.scene: An order changes at short notice before the sample is accepted. Someone checks the item, someone rearranges the schedule, and someone records the changes so shifts can use the same checklist.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Identify who fixes problems on site, who can reschedule delivery, and who owns the standards and change log.
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a real handover with no sensitive information. Write a step each for checking the work, changing the order, and recording what changed.

top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.first_experiment: Spend 30 minutes on a low-risk observation: in the first 10 minutes, bring materials, equipment, samples, or on-site constraints into view; in the next 10 minutes, clarify the goal, resources, next step, and people you need to influence; in the final 10 minutes, clearly organize the steps, fields, rules, or records of checks. Record only which action you most want to continue.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.free_page_teaser: Realistic, Enterprising, and Conventional interest clues can be observed in sequence without rushing to a career answer.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.likely_tension: Differences between the three clues are worth exploring through small tasks. Observing one action and one condition at a time is more reliable than treating the three leading interests as a fixed way of working.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.low_risk_validation: Low-risk observation: choose a small task that accommodates hands-on, moving things forward, and process clues. Record the three activities separately and look only at activity preferences and evidence of wanting to continue.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.ordered_code_handling: The ordered three-letter code describes the reading order for this assessment: the first letter is the initial observation entry point, and the second and third are additional entry points. The order changes what to ask first and what to validate next. It is not a fixed identity, an ability conclusion, or a career answer.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.positive_value: The value of this content is to break the clues into observable small tasks: Realistic focuses on tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results; Enterprising focuses on goals, resources, opportunities, influence, and moving things forward; Conventional focuses on rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records. Whichever comes first only indicates which activity to gather evidence from first. These clues offer exploration questions, not job answers.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.primary_activity_chain: Start with the first dimension, Realistic: use it as the initial observation entry point and look for small-task evidence involving tangible objects, tools, on-site conditions, materials, and visible results.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.real_world_cost: Reading boundary: these three clues may occur in different parts of one task or across different environments. Record only the appeal of specific activities, points of hesitation, and conditions you want to adjust. Do not turn the score order into a ranking of abilities or a fixed way of working.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.secondary_support_line: Then consider the second dimension, Enterprising: use it as an additional observation entry point and record whether goals, resources, opportunities, influence, and moving things forward make the task more appealing.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.strategy_label: Hands-on, moving things forward, and process: three clues to observe
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.tertiary_stabilizer: The third dimension, Conventional, is only an additional clue: observe whether rules, data, processes, order, and reviewable records help distinguish more specific task conditions.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.when_not_to_overread: When response quality is low, the leading scores are close, content is missing, or the user only wants to see the names, return to observing activities rather than offering strong interpretations.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.when_to_use_140q: When a user wants to distinguish whether task activities, environmental conditions, or role responsibilities are more appealing, 140Q can be an option. 140Q only adds contextual detail; it does not increase accuracy or override 60Q.

top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.activity_chain: Observe through three separate activity entry points: analyze questions, evidence, variables, or ways of explaining; try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form; observe real people's needs for understanding, support, communication, or collaboration.
activity_sequence: Initial observation entry point: analyze questions, evidence, variables, or ways of explaining
Second observation entry point: try different approaches to expression, style, narrative, or form
Third observation entry point: observe real people's needs for understanding, support, communication, or collaboration
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.core_reading: These three leading interest dimensions indicate that Investigative, Artistic, and Social activities stand relatively high in this response. They can help organize exploration and questions, but cannot establish a personality identity, ability level, or career conclusion.
top3_code_chain_strategy_v1.en.jsonl.deep_report_extension: Further reading can distinguish preference evidence across tasks, environments, and role responsibilities, and offer exploration questions and follow-up actions.

desktop_reading_v1.career_lens: Research jobs deliver findings people can check. Content jobs deliver materials people can understand. Teaching jobs also need to see what people learn to do. Similar titles can put the emphasis in different places.
desktop_reading_v1.decision: If you most want to check the evidence, look for direct access to source material. If you want to improve the explanation or see someone learn the task, look for access to feedback.
desktop_reading_v1.headline: Find the cause and turn it into something people can use

AIS.career_lens: When looking at content and design jobs, first find out whether you decide what readers see and how they see it. Compare assignments where you rewrite existing material with jobs where you can check the facts, get readers to try it, and revise the presentation.
AIS.decision: If you want to try another format, look for control over revisions and access to feedback. If finding the cause or coaching appeals more, check how much working time goes to those duties.
AIS.headline: Find a clearer way to present something people struggle to understand
AIS.hero_job_tip: Ask whether you can choose how to present the information and revise it in response to what people actually do.
AIS.question: On the last revision, could a newcomer use feedback to compare two versions they made, or did they simply follow the review notes?
AIS.scene: You could turn the same beginner's guide into a diagram or a short demonstration. You might most enjoy deciding what people see first. Compare both versions with new users, then revise the one that helps them follow the steps.
AIS.screen: Find out who decides how to present information and whether the creator can check facts and test it with users.
AIS.trial: Pick a publicly documented step. Make a diagram and a short demonstration. Ask someone to try both and note which leaves fewer pauses.

ASI.career_lens: If you want to design training people will use, find out who chooses the exercises and how to teach them. Check whether you can observe learners and use practice results or feedback to figure out what they missed. That tells you who owns the learning experience.
ASI.decision: If you want to keep breaking down and arranging the content, look for jobs that include design and trial sessions. If you preferred coaching or investigating a misunderstanding, check which jobs give those tasks real time.
ASI.headline: Turn an idea into something people can learn
ASI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether content creators also get to explain the material, lead practice, and make revisions based on what learners actually do.
ASI.question: Once a course is released, can a newcomer observe a practice session and change the order of the material in response to what learners do?
ASI.scene: You might want to turn a dense rule into a practice exercise with a recognizable situation. Walk a newcomer through it and listen to how they interpret it. If several people miss the same line, check whether the explanation or the task itself is getting in the way.
ASI.screen: Look for jobs where you can choose examples and sequence exercises. Check whether you work directly with learners and investigate which steps they haven't mastered.
ASI.trial: Turn a familiar task into a three-minute illustrated guide and do it once with someone. Note which explanation was hardest to follow, revise it, and ask them to explain it back.

IAS.career_lens: Compare what research, content, and teaching roles deliver: a conclusion others can check, instructions a reader can use, or a task a learner can perform independently. Start with jobs where you can investigate the cause and see how people use the findings.
IAS.decision: If you want to keep digging into why people got stuck, favor jobs with direct access to source material. If revising the instructions or helping people get started was more interesting, check whether those tasks recur in the job.
IAS.headline: Get to the bottom of a problem that keeps coming back
IAS.hero_job_tip: Start with roles where you can observe users directly and investigate problems. Ask whether you can help revise the guide once the findings are in.
IAS.question: The last time users got stuck at the same step, what evidence did a newcomer check? After the change was tried, who checked whether it solved the problem?
IAS.scene: New hires have read the guide, yet they keep stopping at the same step. You might first want to know where they get stuck. Watch a few people try it and notice they all mistake the same button for the starting point. Turn the instructions into a diagram and see whether the next new hire can get through on their own.
IAS.screen: Mark the postings that give you access to original material and a chance to investigate where users struggle. Then note whether the role delivers findings, revises instructions, or follows people through onboarding.
IAS.trial: Pick a public guide and ask someone to try one step. Note where they got stuck and what you observed, revise one instruction, and test it again.

ISA.career_lens: In user research or learning evaluation, look for access to first-hand material and the chance to investigate recurring problems. Ask whether you hear where participants got stuck and whether you deliver findings alone or turn them into something people can use.
ISA.decision: If you want to keep investigating and hear from users, look for research with follow-up. If you prefer making something from the findings, find out who decides what the material looks like.
ISA.headline: Find out why everyone asks for help at the same step
ISA.hero_job_tip: Look for roles with access to original support requests and a chance to verify what happened with users.
ISA.question: After several similar requests come in, can a newcomer follow up to confirm the cause? Who turns the findings into clearer guidance?
ISA.scene: Three people say the guide is confusing. You might ask whether they are all running into the same issue. Hear each person describe what they did, separate the different causes behind similar problems, and use that to improve the examples.
ISA.screen: Look for work that investigates difficulties people share. Find out whether you stay in touch with people or turn findings into materials.
ISA.trial: Group three public requests for help and identify one possible cause. Have someone explain their understanding back to you, then draw a visual prompt.

SAI.career_lens: A coaching role may let you rewrite the tutorial, try a new demonstration, and see whether people learned. If the job is mainly measured by how many sessions you complete, check whether it gives you time for those tasks.
SAI.decision: If you want to keep practicing with people, look for coaching time. If creating materials or checking what worked was more interesting, look for jobs that deliver those outputs.
SAI.headline: Find another way to help someone get started
SAI.hero_job_tip: Find out whether you usually coach people directly or deliver material, and whether you have time to check what learners retained.
SAI.question: After coaching someone, can a newcomer rewrite an example and watch them try again?
SAI.scene: If someone reads the guide and still hesitates to try, you might want to sit beside them. Use a different picture or show the steps until they can do it themselves. Check back later to see which support they actually used.
SAI.screen: Look for regular hands-on coaching with room to change explanations. Ask whether the team checks how well people work on their own before and after a change.
SAI.trial: Help someone with a small, safe task. Change one prompt and have them repeat it. Note whether they ask one fewer question.

SIA.career_lens: Look separately at helping people directly and investigating behind the scenes. When someone is stuck at the same step again, do you help them continue or investigate why multiple people get stuck? A role that turns findings into new guidance also involves creating materials.
SIA.decision: If you want to stay with someone and see their progress, keep ongoing support roles. If you most want to find a common cause, look for access to original feedback.
SIA.headline: Trace why someone couldn't get the hang of a task
SIA.hero_job_tip: Look for roles that let you follow up with learners. Ask whether you can investigate repeated difficulties and who revises the materials.
SIA.question: When several people struggle with the same task, does a newcomer have time to follow cases, investigate the shared problem, and revise the help material?
SIA.scene: You might care most about whether a new colleague can do the task back at their desk. Listen to why they stopped, compare that with the difficulties others reported, and rewrite the prompt in a form that addresses the actual problem.
SIA.screen: Start with jobs that answer questions or coach people directly. Find out whether you can investigate similar problems and turn the findings into visual materials.
SIA.trial: Ask someone about a recent difficulty learning a task. Ask two questions to clarify what happened and sketch a prompt they can use immediately.

desktop_reading_v1.question: After the last time users got stuck, did a newcomer get to observe, revise the instructions, or follow up to see what users learned?
desktop_reading_v1.scene: Several new hires say the guide is hard to follow. After watching people use it twice, you see they're looking for a button the instructions never identify. Break the procedure into three images and circle the entry point. The next person can finish on their own. This work gives you a chance to investigate, explain, and see what people do with the result.
desktop_reading_v1.screen: Compare what you would deliver most often: evidence, visual or written materials, or helping people learn a task. Similar job titles can have very different mixes.
desktop_reading_v1.trial: Pick a public guide. Find one step that could be misunderstood, write one sentence explaining why, and draw a clearer version.

Record only which action you most want to continue.
